# Probation Prep Pack — AI Engineer
_Four sub-artefacts. Self-assessment, pre-review 1:1, evidence portfolio (with the calibration log), worked conversation playbook. Rehearse last._

## Sub-artefact 1: Self-Assessment

One page. Three columns.

| Built | Calibrated | Want next |
|-------|------------|-----------|
_'Built' (what you shipped — evals, prompts, features); 'Calibrated' (moments you said 'no, not yet' or made the conservative call against hype). Three to five items per column._

## Sub-artefact 2: Pre-Review 1:1 Agenda

Thirty minutes, booked a week before the formal review. Framing:

> 'I want to walk into our review ready. Specifically, I want to know which of my calls this quarter you'd defend with me, and which ones you'd have made differently — including the no's I held.'

The AIE-specific reframe is asking the manager to be candid about calibration calls, not just technical output. AIE managers are often technical themselves; they will engage with the technical reasoning honestly.

### Agenda

1. **My read of the quarter's technical work** (3 min). One paragraph.
2. **The hardest call I made and the call I'm least sure about** (5 min).
3. **Your read — which calls you'd defend, which you'd revisit** (15 min). Listen.
4. **What 'a strong AIE in this team' looks like a year in** (5 min).
5. **What you'd like me to surface in the formal review** (2 min).

## Sub-artefact 3: Evidence Portfolio (with the Calibration Log)

Two parts: shipped technical work, AND the calibration log — moments you held a 'no, not yet' or made a conservative call against the trade-press fashion.

### Shipped (3-5 items, with the production impact each one had)

| Item | Date | Production impact | What was technically interesting |
|------|------|-------------------|----------------------------------|
|      |      |                   |                                  |

### Calibration log (3-5 items)

| Moment | What the hype said to do | What I did | Outcome |
|--------|--------------------------|------------|---------|
|        |                          |            |         |

_The calibration log is the AIE-signature artefact. The reviewer wants to see you resist hype without being a reflexive contrarian._

## Sub-artefact 4: The Conversation Playbook

_See the annotated worked example below._

# The AI Engineer Probation Review — Worked Example

_Setting: Adisa Okafor (Director of Engineering, AI line) and the AIE. Day 88. Thirty minutes. The AIE has strong production signal: the agentic-vs-feature defence in week 11, the RAG-vs-fine-tune call in front of the CFO in week 7, the Friday-hallucination incident handled cleanly in week 10, 12 evals built in 90 days, the cost-analysis that landed Henrietta's board number._

---

**Adisa:** Tell me about a moment this quarter where you knew the answer was 'no, this isn't going to work' — and you said it.

_[**AIE's silent thought:** The agentic-vs-feature defence is the cleanest example. Lead with it; the temptation to follow the trade-press pattern was real, and saying no to Tomasz (after he'd become my ally on evals) was genuinely hard.]_

**AIE:** The agentic-vs-feature defence in week 11. Tomasz argued for rebuilding the customer-support assistant as an agentic system; the trade press is full of agentic patterns right now and I think Tomasz was reading some of it. I pushed back on the build for this system at this stage.

_[**Annotation:** Names the moment specifically. Doesn't claim 'I'm against agents' — frames it as 'this system, this stage'. The calibration is in the specificity.]_

**Adisa:** Walk me through the reasoning.

**AIE:** Four well-defined capabilities, not ten. The agentic overhead is real: ~2× tokens per response, harder evals (the LLM's tool-choice becomes a thing we have to test), and a class of hallucination we don't currently have — the LLM calling the wrong tool. The flexibility benefit is real but kicks in around 10+ capabilities. We have four. If we get to eight and we're still adding more, the agentic refactor is the right call then; right now, the feature shape is.

_[**Annotation:** Numbers, not vibes. '2× tokens' is specific. 'Around 10+ capabilities' is the calibration. The AIE who can name the revisit trigger is the AIE who's calibrating, not opposing.]_

**Adisa:** And Tomasz?

**AIE:** Tomasz heard it cleanly. I didn't put him in a defensive position — the framing was about the system, not about who proposed the alternative. He sent me a Slack two days later saying he'd been reading the agent-framework documentation more carefully and he agreed with the call. The decision's in ADR-016 with the trigger written down.

_[**Annotation:** Names the relationship surviving. The week-6 eval pushback with Tomasz was the start of that relationship; the week-11 agentic conversation was the test of it. The AIE is signalling they handle technical disagreement without making it personal.]_

**Adisa:** What's the one you're least sure about?

_[**AIE's silent thought:** She's asking specifically for honest uncertainty. The cost-analysis work for Henrietta is probably the right answer — I committed to a number that I think is right, but the per-user usage distribution is from a 3-week beta and could change materially with broader rollout.]_

**AIE:** The cost analysis for the board in week 9. The $1.18/user/month number is defensible given the 3-week beta data, but the per-user usage distribution is right-skewed and could shift materially when we roll out beyond the 40 beta users. I told Henrietta about the sensitivity range in the doc; I'm not sure I emphasised it enough. If we hit 400 users and the top decile uses more than I projected, we could be off by 30-50% on the headline. I'd want to revisit at month 3 of broader rollout with real data.

_[**Annotation:** Specific uncertainty. Named the assumption that's fragile. Named the trigger for the revisit. Doesn't disclaim the number itself — defends the methodology, names the limit.]_

**Adisa:** That's the right answer. Most AIEs at your stage would either defend the number absolutely or apologise for it. You've done neither.

_[**Annotation:** Adisa is signalling. The AIE found the calibration she's testing for: defend the methodology, name the uncertainty, propose the revisit.]_

**Adisa:** OK. We're standing up a new AI team for the partner-integrations work in Q3. I'm thinking about who leads the eval-and-cost-discipline side of it. Would you want that?

**AIE:** I'd want it. I'd want to pair with someone more senior than me on it for the first six weeks — the partner-integrations work has external SLAs I haven't navigated yet, and I'd want to learn how Tomasz or one of the staff engineers does that side. After six weeks I'd own it.

_[**Annotation:** Accepts the offer. Names what they'd want to learn first. Acknowledges the specific gap (external-SLA-shaped work) — that's a real gap, not false modesty. The 'after six weeks I'd own it' is the specificity that distinguishes confidence from over-eagerness.]_

**Adisa:** Let me see what I can land. Day 90 conversation is the formality. Welcome to the team.

---

_The AIE walked out with an effective 'yes' though the formal Day-90 conversation was still ahead. 'Welcome to the team' is the closest thing to direct confirmation Adisa was going to give. The next-quarter assignment is already being arranged._

annotations.note: Self-assessment uses 'Built' AND 'Calibrated' as the first two columns. The AIE's value is both the building AND the calibration; the columns reflect that. Without the 'Calibrated' column, the assessment reads as output-volume.

Pre-review 1:1 reframe pulls candidness about calibration calls. AIE managers are typically technical themselves; they will engage with the reasoning honestly — and they will respect the AIE who asks for that honesty up front.

The calibration log is the AIE-signature artefact. Three to five moments where you said 'no, not yet' or made the conservative call. Without this section, the portfolio reads as 'AIE who built things' (volume); with it, the portfolio reads as 'AIE who made calls' (judgement).

The annotated conversation shows: lead with the hardest no, defend with numbers not vibes, name the revisit trigger, name your own uncertainty without disclaiming the work. The AIE-specific moves: don't perform anti-pattern stance; calibrate against the system + stage.

common_mistakes: Self-assessment lists shipped features only. The AIE's value is both building AND calibration; the assessment must reflect both.
Calibration log omitted. The most common AIE-probation-pack failure. Without it, the reviewer sees output volume, not the judgement work.
Couldn't name a 'no, not yet' moment. Adisa-class reviewers are specifically testing for this; absence reads as hype-matching.
Defending technical calls with 'industry best practice' citations rather than specific reasoning about this system + this stage.

Treating uncertainty as something to minimise. Adisa rewarded the AIE for naming a specific sensitivity (the per-user usage distribution) without disclaiming the methodology. False confidence is more disqualifying than calibrated uncertainty.
Bringing a printed pack and walking it through. The pack enables the conversation; presenting it wastes the conversation.
variant_patterns: Extended-probation variant: the conversation playbook reshapes around 'what specifically would land as continued in the next 30 days?' — pulling behavioural specifics about technical work.

First-AIE-on-the-team variant (team had no dedicated AIE before): the evidence portfolio shifts to include 'practices I introduced' (eval rubrics, cost analyses, model cards, ADRs) alongside features built. The probation review will partly assess whether the role's existence is justified.
Senior-AIE-being-promoted-to-staff variant: the calibration log becomes the dominant evidence section; the technical-build evidence is assumed and not central. Different role, different conversation.
